query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, the dynamic mechanical response is controlled by a transition between diffusion‐mediated dynamic strain aging at lower strain rates (and/or intermediate temperatures) and phonon drag–dominated dislocation motion at very high strain rates. In other words, when there is sufficient time for solute atoms to locally pin dislocations (leading to serrated flow and moderate strengthening), the alloy shows moderate strain rate sensitivity; but as the strain rate increases toward the dynamic regime (≥10^3 s⁻¹), the thermal activation time becomes too short, so that phonon drag effects take over, leading to a pronounced jump in yield strength and altered serration features.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully solidified, single-phase FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy in a homogeneous disordered solid-solution state (analogous to its equiatomic precursor but with Co removed).
generation.intervention: Apply mechanical deformation tests at controlled strain rates, ranging from quasi‐static (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) to dynamic (≥10³ s⁻¹), at fixed temperatures (e.g., room temperature and/or at a lower temperature where diffusion is slower).
generation.conditions: The tests should be conducted within the solid solution regime (i.e., before any dynamic recrystallization or phase transformations occur) and at temperatures low enough that no recovery or softening mechanisms (such as DRX) are activated, but high enough to permit some solute mobility for dynamic strain aging at low rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Mobile dislocations interacting with local solute atmospheres that can form and dissolve (Cottrell atmospheres) as well as with lattice vibrations (phonons) that produce viscous drag. The density and arrangement of dislocations (evidenced by serration patterns in stress–strain curves) serve as mediators of the transition.
generation.mechanism: At lower strain rates, there is sufficient time for solute atoms to migrate and transiently pin moving dislocations, generating periodic bursts of motion (serrations) and moderate work hardening—a hallmark of dynamic strain aging. Conversely, at very high strain rates the reduced time for atomic diffusion and thermal activation causes dislocation motion to be impeded primarily by phonon drag; this results in a larger effective yield strength and a qualitatively different serration pattern (if any), since the dislocations overcome resistance not via solute unpinning but by surmounting the viscous drag force.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline quasi‐static condition (e.g., deformation at 10⁻³ s⁻¹), the alloy will exhibit a marked increase in yield strength and a shift or amplification in serration amplitude once the strain rate exceeds a threshold (on the order of 10³ s⁻¹). Furthermore, the temperature dependence of these effects should reveal that, at a fixed high strain rate, the contribution from phonon drag becomes more pronounced at higher temperatures, while serration behavior associated with dynamic strain aging diminishes.
generation.baseline: Quasi‐static deformation (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) at a standard temperature (e.g., room temperature) where dynamic strain aging dominates and no significant phonon drag is observed.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic model is applicable for the alloy in its as-cast, single-phase solid-solution state when no phase transformations (such as DRX or precipitation) or other microstructural changes intervene. It assumes temperatures below those at which recovery and recrystallization mechanisms begin to dominate (i.e., below ~700 °C) and strain rates ranging from quasi‐static to extreme dynamic rates.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis combines evidence of strain-rate-dependent serration behavior and phonon drag effects from studies on CoCrFeMnNi HEAs (e.g., PMC7512474::web::002, PMC7512474::web::012, and PMC7512474::web::014) and extends these mechanisms to the Co-free derivative. It is uncertain how the removal of Co affects solute diffusion kinetics and the balance between dynamic strain aging and phonon drag in this new composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of deformation tests on the Co-free FeNiCrMn HEA at a constant temperature (e.g., room temperature) while systematically varying the strain rate from quasi-static (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) to a high dynamic regime (≥10³ s⁻¹). Compare the stress-strain curves for serration characteristics and yield strength. In parallel, conduct tests at a lower temperature (where atomic mobility is reduced) to assess the sensitivity of serration behavior to thermal activation. Additionally, use high-speed imaging and in-situ microscopy (if possible) to capture dislocation dynamics during deformation.
measurements: Amplitude and frequency of serrations in the stress-strain curves
In-situ observations or post-mortem dislocation density and arrangement (via TEM or other high-resolution techniques)
Temperature dependence of these features at fixed high strain rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, as the strain rate increases from quasi-static to dynamic regimes, the yield strength does not show the predicted sharp increase and the serration patterns do not change in a manner consistent with a shift from dynamic strain aging to phonon drag domination, then the hypothesis must be rejected. Similarly, if the temperature dependence of these features does not match the expected trends (i.e., diminished dynamic strain aging signals at elevated temperatures and no clear indication of phonon drag effects), then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: He et al. [] studied the stress exponent (the reciprocal of strain rate sensitivity) of the NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy deformed under strain rates less than 10−2 s−1. He found that the stress exponent was in a positive relationship with the strain rates. When the strain rate ranged from 3.205 × 10−5 to 8.013 × 10−4 s−1, the stress exponent increased simultaneously. Moon et al. [] also studied the strain rate sensitivity at the elevated temperature and the cryogenic temperature, respectively. The results showed that the flow stress at 77 K was higher than that at room temperature. Therefore, the strain rate sensitivity of the flow stress at RT was higher than that at 77 K under strain rates less than 1 × 10−2 s−1. cited_evidence.kind: web:4.2. Mechanism for the Serration Behavior
cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys present serrations on the flow stress curves during the plastic deformation, often at a normal strain rate around 1 × 10−4 s−1 or at low temperatures. Serration behavior exhibits in the stress-strain curves of the Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi high-entropy alloy at 7 K, 7.5 K, and 9 K at a strain rate of 4 × 10−4 s−1 []. The Al5Cr12Fe35Mn28Ni20 high-entropy alloy exhibits typical serration behaviors at the elevated temperatures of 573 K and 673 K, with a strain rate of 1 × 10−4 s−1 []. Several microstructure mechanisms are proposed to explain the serration behavior, e.g., the Portevin-Le Chatelier (PLC) effect. Serration behavior was supposed to be associated with Cottrell atmosphere interaction with moving dislocations, slip bands, and dynamic strain aging. In Figure 4, it can be seen that the stress-strain curves of the as-cast NiCrFeCoMn high-entropy alloy deformed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1 show no serrations, and marked serrations are present on the stress-strain curves of specimens deformed at strain rates above 900 s−1.
